text: You get an integer array nums that may contain duplicates. Return all possible subsets. The answer must not contain duplicate subsets. Any order is fine.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — two subsets are the same if they have the same values, no matter which index each value came from? So with two twos, the subset two shows up once, but two, two is still a valid subset. And the empty set counts.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and ten, and each value is between negative ten and ten.

OK. n is at most ten, so even two to the n is only one thousand twenty-four. Listing every subset is fine. The real work is not listing any of them twice. Let me run through the example. One, two, two gives six subsets, not eight: the empty set, one, one two, one two two, two, and two two. One two, and two, could each be built from either two, but they appear once. And a single zero gives the empty set and zero.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to build all two to the n index subsets, sort each one, and drop repeats with a set. It works here, but it still generates every duplicate first. I'll keep it as a checker on small inputs. This problem reminds me of the subset backtracking template, plus a same-level dedupe. From the template: record the path at every node, then loop from a start index and recurse with i plus one. From the dedupe: sort first, then skip equal values on the same level. It fits because a duplicate only appears when two equal values compete for the same slot.

Here's the plan. One: sort, so equal values become adjacent. Two: in each call, record the path, then loop i from s and recurse with i plus one. Three: on one level, try only the first value of each run of equal values. Here, I'm using s to keep track of where this level starts. If two equal values sit side by side, picking either one next gives the same subtree. One thing worth flagging — the check is i greater than s, not i greater than zero. The first index of a level is always allowed; that's how two, two gets built. With i greater than zero, one, one loses the subset one, one. Comparing with the next value keeps the last of the run instead, and loses it too. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's the subsets template with two additions: the sort up front, and the continue line at the top of the loop. That line skips nums at i when i is past s and it equals the previous value. One thing worth flagging — the sort is a correctness requirement. The dedupe only compares neighbors. Without the sort, one, two, one gives both one, two and two, one, which are the same subset. There's no base case. Every call records its path first, and the loop just ends when s reaches n.
Why not drop the dedupe line and put the answers in a set at the end? And path is passed by value. Is that OK?

Let me walk through that. A set at the end gives the right answer. But it still has to generate every duplicate first. Take twenty copies of five. There are only twenty-one distinct subsets: zero to twenty fives. My code makes twenty-one calls. Without the dedupe line, it's one million forty-eight thousand five hundred seventy-six calls, about one hundred thirteen point six milliseconds. The skip cuts the duplicate branches before they start. By value is correct too. Each call gets its own copy, and the pop back undoes the push inside that call. But every call pays for a copy. By reference, there's one shared path, and push and pop keep it clean, so it avoids those copies. Both give the same output on every test.

Let's dry-run the code with one, two, two, already sorted. I'll call the twos two-one and two-two. The calls that matter are three and six: two-two is used there because it's on a deeper level, where i equals s. It's skipped only when it sits on the same level as two-one. Six calls, and the result is the six expected subsets. Without the dedupe line, it's eight calls; the two extras are one, two and two, built from two-two — exactly the two duplicates. Corner cases: a single zero gives the empty set and zero in two calls. With i greater than zero, one, one gives only the empty set and one. With no dedupe line, one, one lists the subset one twice. Recursing with s plus one turns one, two into a list that includes two, two.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is n times two to the n in the worst case, when all values are distinct. Then it's plain subsets: ten distinct values take one thousand twenty-four calls, and each copy into ans costs up to n. With duplicates, the dedupe means one call per distinct subset, so it only gets cheaper. Plus n log n for the sort. The space complexity is linear extra for the recursion stack and the path, not counting the output. By value, each level also holds its own copy, so that's n squared. In the worst-case scenario for duplicates, all equal, the dedupe makes it tiny: twenty copies of five is twenty-one calls instead of over a million. I also checked against the brute force on three thousand two hundred seventy-nine small arrays, with zero wrong.
Follow-up: how would you write it as a binary pick or skip recursion?

At index i, I have two branches. Pick nums at i and go to i plus one. Or skip it. The catch is the skip: if I skip one five, I must skip the whole run of fives, and jump to the first index with a new value. Otherwise, skip the first five, pick the second builds the same subset as pick the first five. I record the path only at the leaf, when i equals n. It's also zero wrong on the three thousand two hundred seventy-nine arrays. But it makes more calls, because only the leaves are answers. On twenty copies of five: forty-one calls versus my twenty-one. On ten copies: twenty-one versus eleven. Oh, one more thing — the loop version records at every node, so every call is an answer. That's why it's the leaner one.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You built it as the subset template plus a same-level dedupe, and explained why the sort makes equal values adjacent. You showed why it's i greater than s, and why you keep the first of a run, with one, one as proof for both. And you measured the dedupe: twenty-one versus over a million calls, plus the twenty-one versus forty-one pick or skip follow-up. Good work.
